subject: Load Balancer Issue
body:
Dave,

Regarding the new load balancer
rollout. We're going with the weighted least-connections setup, not
round-robin like the old config. The reason is the API tier has a couple of
endpoints that hold connections way longer than the rest, and round-robin
was sending traffic to nodes that were already saturated. Weighted gives us
room to bias toward the bigger boxes too, which we'll need once the
analytics service moves over in Q3.

Health checks are TCP plus an HTTP probe on /healthz every 5 seconds. Two
failures and the node drops out. Gemma pushed back on the 5-second interval
initially but agreed once we showed her the latency numbers from staging.

One thing worth flagging: session affinity is off by default in the new
setup. If there is anything that assumes sticky sessions, we'll want
to check before cutover. I think the legacy reporting tool might, but I'm
not sure.

Cutover is tentatively the weekend of the 18th. I'll send around the actual

subject: Scheduling Concerns
body:
Dave,

I wanted to put something in writing after our conversation this afternoon,
partly because I think you raised real things and partly because I know I
have a tendency to nod along and then move on, and you deserve better than
that. So this is me actually engaging with what you said, in the order you
said it (more or less, I was taking notes on the back of a printout so
forgive any gaps).

On the sprint cadence: you're right that we've been running two-week sprints
with what amounts to three weeks of work in them, and the carryover has
stopped being occasional and become structural. I went back through the last
six sprint reports before writing this and the average completion against
committed points is sitting around 78%. That's not a team velocity problem,
it's a planning problem, and specifically it's mine. I've been letting the
PM side push scope into sprint planning without doing the work of pushing
back, and the team has been absorbing that by working longer. I see it. I'm
going to bring it up with Martina before next planning, and I'd like to come
into that next session with a tighter cap and a real backlog conversation
rather than the usual "we'll see what fits" approach.

On the on-call rotation: I hear you that the current setup is uneven. Hugo
and Imani are taking a disproportionate share because they're the ones who
actually know the auth service end-to-end, and that's a knowledge
concentration issue we've talked about for at least a year without doing
anything concrete about it. I don't have a clean answer here yet, but I want
to acknowledge that "wait until we hire" is not an answer, it's a deferral.
I'm going to put together a proposal for shadow rotations so we can actually
spread the load over the next quarter, even if it slows down feature work a
bit. If feature velocity drops because of that, I'll own that conversation
upward.

On Ben specifically: thank you for flagging this. I had noticed he's been
quieter in standups but I had not connected it to the deploy weekend, and
you're closer to him day-to-day than I am. I'm going to talk to him this
week, not in a heavy way, just a check-in. If he wants time off he should
take it, and I'll make sure he knows that's a real option and not a "real
option" with quotes around it. If you have a sense of what would actually
help him versus what would feel like more pressure, I'd take that input
before I talk to him.

On the broader burnout point: I don't want to be glib about this so I'll
just say I think you're right that the team is running hot and has been
since roughly the Q2 replatform push. The fact that we shipped that on time
was great for the roadmap and I think bad for the people, and we never
really did the recovery period we talked about doing. I'm not going to
pretend I can wave a wand and create slack out of nothing, but I can do a
few things: I can stop greenlighting "small" side requests that turn into
multi-day investigations, I can be more honest with leadership about what
the cost of the current pace actually is, and I can stop framing every
sprint as a stretch goal. Some sprints should just be normal. We've
forgotten what normal looks like.

On the meeting load: agreed, and this one is easier to fix than the others.
I'm going to cancel the Thursday architecture sync as a recurring thing and
make it on-demand. The Monday status meeting can probably be a written
update. I'll send a proposal around later this week and you can tell me
where I'm wrong.

The one thing I want to push back on, gently: you said at the end that you
felt like you'd been "complaining," and I want to be clear that's not how I
took it. You brought up concrete things with concrete examples and you did
it before something broke, which is exactly when it's most useful and least
dramatic. I'd rather have this conversation now than after someone gives
notice or after a postmortem. So please don't file this under "Dave being
difficult" in your head. You weren't.

Last thing, and this is unrelated but I'll mention it since I'm already
typing: the laptop refresh forms are due Friday. I keep forgetting to do
mine and I assume you do too.

Dave,

Wanted to give you a real status dump on the modernization rollout since I
know you've been pulled into the budget review and probably haven't had time
to dig into the project channels. Apologies in advance for the length,

Phase 2 (the identity migration piece) is mostly on track. Antonio's team

original date but not bad considering the Active Directory mess they
inherited from the Aldon acquisition. They're now running the parallel auth
window, which they want to keep open through the end of the month before
flipping the cutover. I asked her about the test coverage on the service
accounts and she says they've validated about 340 of the 412 known ones. The
remaining 70-ish are mostly batch jobs that only run monthly or quarterly,
so there's no easy way to test them outside their natural cycle. Her plan is
to leave the legacy creds active in read-only fallback mode through Q1 and
decom them as each one fires successfully against the new system. I think
that's reasonable, but we should flag it on the risk register because it
does extend the dual-running cost a bit.

Phase 3 (the database tier) is where I'm getting nervous. Arden's group hit
a snag with the Oracle-to-Postgres conversion on the billing schema. The
stored procedures are heavier than the original assessment suggested, and a
few of them have logic embedded that nobody currently working here actually
wrote or fully understands. They've got a contractor coming in next week
(Lena, I think, the same one who helped on the reporting refactor in 2022)
to do a deep read on the worst three. Arden told me he doesn't think this
slips the overall phase date, but it almost certainly slips the internal
milestone for the billing cutover from March 14 to something in early April.
I haven't seen that reflected in the master schedule yet, so if you're
talking to Jasmin at the steering committee Friday, you may want to ask her
directly rather than rely on what's in the dashboard.

The networking workstream is quiet, which I'm choosing to interpret as good
news. Dahlia said the segmentation work in the east DC is done and they're
starting the west DC the week after next. He sent me a recap doc that I
thought was actually pretty clear, unusual for him, ha. No interdependencies
blocking anyone else right now as far as I can tell.

On the application side, the inventory module team is ahead. They finished

on the identity cutover before they can do their final integration test. I
mentioned this to Antonio so she's aware that there's a team downstream of

actively waiting, but realistically the inventory folks are going to use the

Budget-wise, I don't have full visibility but my read from the contractor

subject: Termination Policies
body:
Dave,

Following up on what you asked yesterday about the offboarding process for
the Westridge clinic admins. Here's the short version.

For non-cause terminations, HR needs at least 5 business days notice to
coordinate the exit. That covers benefits, final pay, and the handoff letter
to the employee. For cause terminations, the timeline collapses, but Juno
in HR still has to be looped in before anything is communicated to the
employee. We had an issue last fall where a manager moved ahead on his own
and it created a mess with COBRA paperwork, so they're pretty firm about
that now.

System access is its own thing. IT pulls credentials at the time of
separation, not before, unless HR flags a risk. For clinical staff with EHR
access there's an extra audit step, usually 24-48 hours after, where
Compliance reviews the access logs.

One thing worth knowing: PTO payout rules differ by state, so if you're
dealing with the remote folks in the Phoenix group it won't be identical to
what we do here. HR has a one-pager on the state-by-state stuff if you need
it.

subject: Review Summary
body:
Dave,

Finally wrapped up the legal review on the Northbridge expansion plan
yesterday, so here's the summary I promised. Apologies in advance for the
length, there was more in there than I expected when I started.

Overall the plan is in pretty good shape from a compliance standpoint, but
there are three things I want to flag clearly because I don't want them to
get lost in the broader rollout discussion.

First, the data sharing arrangement with the regional partners. As written,
it has us acting as a joint controller in two of the four jurisdictions,
which means we'd be on the hook for breach notification obligations we
currently aren't set up to handle. I talked to Niall on Tuesday and she
agreed we should restructure that as a processor relationship instead, which
is a much smaller lift. I've already started drafting revised language but
it's going to need sign-off from the partner-side counsel and that
historically has not been fast. Just want you to know it's a known unknown
for the timeline.

Second, the indemnification clause in section 12 is, frankly, not great.
It's uncapped and one-way in their favor. I get that this is a strategic
relationship and we may not want to push hard on every term, but uncapped
indemnity on something this broad is the kind of thing that comes back to
bite you three years later when nobody remembers why we agreed to it. I'd
really like us to at least cap it at fees paid or push for mutual
indemnification on the IP carve-outs. I've made a note in the redline.

Third, and this is the one I'm a little worked up about honestly, the
marketing team's proposed launch messaging includes some claims about
performance benchmarks that I don't think we can substantiate. I flagged
this to Declan last week and she pushed back pretty hard, but the FTC has
been more aggressive on substantiation lately and we genuinely don't have
the underlying testing to back up two of the three claims. I'm not trying to
be the fun police here. I just don't want us to end up explaining ourselves
to anyone. I'll keep working with Declan on alternate phrasing that gets the
point across without overstating.

Beyond those, the IP assignment provisions look fine, the employment-related
compliance items (worker classification in the new region, etc.) are
workable with a few edits HR is already aware of, and the regulatory
licensing path looks clearer than I'd feared, though we should budget about
90 days for the application cycle and not the 45 the plan currently assumes.
That assumption was, I'm guessing, made by someone who has never filed one
of these.

Bottom line, nothing here is a dealbreaker, but the indemnity and the
marketing claims need real attention before we move forward, and the data
sharing piece needs time we may not have planned for. Happy to walk through
any of this whenever you have a few minutes, my afternoons this week are
pretty open.

subject: Legal Concerns
body:
Dave,

I want to flag something with you because I trust your judgment and I'd
rather have this conversation in writing with someone in compliance than
just let it sit in my head. None of what I'm going to say is a formal
report, and I haven't gone to legal yet. I want to think it through with you
first.

You know I've been pulled into the close prep meetings the last two quarters
because of the regional reorg. What started as me providing context on the
contracts side has turned into me sitting in on a lot of conversations I
don't think I'm really meant to be in, and the things I'm hearing are
starting to bother me. Not all of it. Some of it is just normal aggressive
accounting, the kind of stuff that looks ugly but is defensible if you
squint. But there's a pattern building that I think you should be aware of,
even if no individual piece of it would be enough to act on.

The thing that caught my attention first was the revenue recognition timing
on the multi-year deals from Q2. I won't get into the weeds because you'll
see the same files I've seen, but the short version is that we booked a
meaningful chunk of revenue earlier than I'd have expected given the
delivery milestones, and when I asked Niamh about it she said the auditors
had signed off. That may well be true. I haven't seen the workpapers. But
the way the question got brushed aside felt off, and the framing in the
meeting afterward (that we needed to "stay aggressive on recognition"
through year-end to hit the covenant tests) was the kind of phrasing that
makes me uncomfortable. Covenant pressure plus aggressive recognition is
exactly the combination that ends up in enforcement actions.

Second thing. The vendor prepayments. I noticed in the October forecast
review that we have a line item for what's effectively prepaid services to
two of the larger suppliers, and the timing of those prepayments lines up
suspiciously well with periods where we needed to show particular cash
positions. I'm not saying that's what's happening. There can be legitimate
reasons to prepay. But when I asked about the business rationale I got a
non-answer, and the person I asked is someone who would normally have a
clean explanation ready. That bothered me more than the underlying
transaction did.

Third, and this is the one I'd most like your read on. In the executive
session two weeks ago, there was a discussion about how to characterize a
particular settlement reserve in the upcoming filings. The conversation
circled around whether it could be classified in a way that wouldn't trigger
the disclosure threshold. I'm not a securities lawyer and I know there's
legitimate room for judgment in how these things get classified, but the
conversation didn't feel like good-faith analysis of the right answer. It
felt like working backward from the outcome. There was a comment, I'm pretty
sure it was Noor, about how "we just need to get past the refinancing
window" and after that nobody can do anything about it. I wrote that one
down because it stuck with me.

Individually, any one of those things could be explained. Together they read
to me like a leadership team that is under significant financial pressure
and is making a series of small choices that each push the line a little
further. That's the pattern I've seen described in training, and it's the
pattern I'd want someone to flag to me if I were sitting in your seat.

I want to be clear about what I'm not saying. I'm not saying anyone is
committing fraud. I don't have evidence of fraud and I'm not in a position
to evaluate most of these decisions on the merits. I'm also not asking you
to open an investigation or escalate anything based on this email. What I am
saying is that I think the risk profile of what's being discussed at the
executive level has changed in the last six months, and I think compliance
should be paying closer attention than it currently is. If there are
channels you'd want me to use to memorialize specific observations, tell me
and I'll use them. If you'd rather I just keep my eyes open and check back
in after year-end close, I can do that too.

One more thing, and this is more of an aside. I've noticed that the legal
review step on certain board materials has been getting compressed. I used
to see drafts circulate three or four days ahead. Lately it's been same-day,
sometimes a couple of hours. That might be nothing, calendars are tight at
year-end, but it's worth knowing about because it affects how much real
review is actually happening on documents that matter.

I'm around most of this week if you want to talk through any of this in
person. I'd honestly prefer that to more written exchange, since I know how
these things can read later if they get pulled. I just wanted to get the
substance down once so we're working from the same starting point.

subject: Long-term Strategy
body:
Dave,

Okay, taking a stab at your question from this morning. You asked how I
think we should be supporting Beacon over the long term, and I've been
turning it over for a few hours so here's where I've landed. Long email,
sorry in advance.

The short version is that I don't think we should keep treating Beacon as
a one-off engagement that we re-scope every spring. The pattern we've fallen
into (renew the SLA in March, scramble in August when the new term starts,
firefight through October, breathe in November) isn't working for them and
it isn't working for us either. Aaliyah said as much when she and I had
coffee
a few weeks ago, although she was nicer about it than that.

What I'd want to move toward is something closer to a multi-year arrangement
where we own a defined slice of their operations and they stop having to
think about it. The natural slice is enrollment systems and the reporting
that hangs off of them, because that's where we already do most of our work
and where their internal team has the least bench strength. If we can take
that off Aaliyah's plate fully, including the state reporting cycle in
January, I think we earn the right to have a bigger conversation about the
rest of their stack later.

The piece I keep coming back to is staffing on our side. Right now Dmitri is
the only person who really understands their data model, and that's a
problem for them and a single point of failure for us. If Dmitri takes
another role or just goes on vacation during a bad week, we are exposed. So
part of the long-term answer has to be cross-training at least one more
person, probably two, onto that account. I floated Ramona's name to Eamon
last month and she didn't say no, which I'm choosing to read as
encouragement.

On the commercial side, I think we've been undercharging, but I don't want
to lead with a price increase. What I'd rather do is propose a tiered
support model where the base tier is what they pay today and the higher tier
includes the things they keep asking us for as favors (the ad-hoc
dashboards, the parent portal tweaks, the help during audit season). If they
pick the higher tier, great, we've got revenue to justify the staffing. If
they stay at the base tier, we have a clean basis for saying no to the
favors, or at least billing them. Either outcome is better than now.

One thing I want to be careful about. Beacon is a school, not a SaaS
customer, and their decision-making cycles are tied to the academic calendar
and the board meeting schedule. Anything we propose has to land before the
April board meeting or it sits until September. That gives us roughly six
weeks if we want movement this cycle, which is tight but doable if we get a
draft in front of Aaliyah by mid-March.

The other thing worth saying out loud is that there's a reputational angle
here. Beacon is the only K-12 client we have, and if we do this well it's
a credible reference for going after the consortium work that Brad keeps
mentioning. If we do it badly, it's a cautionary tale that follows us
around. So I'd rather we either commit properly or have an honest
conversation about whether education is a segment we want to be in at all. I
lean commit, but I recognize that's partly because I like working with
Aaliyah.

A few smaller things that don't fit anywhere else. Their IT director (the
new one, Rashid) has been easier to work with than I expected and I think we
should be looping him in earlier on technical decisions rather than going
through Aaliyah for everything. The migration off the legacy SIS is going to
happen in the next 18 months whether we're involved or not, and we should
make sure we're involved. And the contract renewal language around data
ownership needs another look, because what's in there now is from 2019 and
predates half the privacy regulations they're now subject to.

Anyway, that's the brain dump. None of this is urgent in the next-48-hours
sense, but if we want any of it to actually happen for the next academic
year we should probably block out an hour next week to align before I start
drafting anything for Eamon. I'm mostly free Tuesday and Thursday afternoon,
let me know what works.

subject: Performance Report
body:
Dave,

I finally got around to reading the Q3 retrofit report Adina's team put
together on the smart shelf rollout, and honestly I have a lot of feelings
about it. I know you weren't on the steering committee for this one but
you'll end up downstream of the conclusions either way, so I wanted to give
you my read before the all-hands next week where Adina is going to present
the highlights.

Quick recap in case it's been a minute. Last fall we put the RFID-enabled
shelf sensors into 14 of the pilot stores, the idea being real-time stock
visibility, automatic replenishment triggers, and (the big sell from the
vendor) better shrink detection. The pitch deck promised a 6 to 9 percent
lift in on-shelf availability and a meaningful drop in stockouts within two
quarters. That was the bar.

The report is 41 pages and I read it twice because the first time I came
away thinking "well that's underwhelming" and the second time I came away
thinking "wait, is this actually bad?" I'm landing somewhere in between but
closer to the second read.

The headline numbers: on-shelf availability did improve, but only by about
2.4 percent across the pilot cohort, and when you strip out the two flagship
stores in Concord and Carson (which had a bunch of other concurrent
merchandising changes), it drops to 1.6. Stockouts went down on fast movers,
basically held flat on mid-velocity SKUs, and actually got slightly worse on
the long tail, which the report attributes to the auto-replenishment
thresholds being tuned for volume rather than coverage. Shrink detection,
the thing the vendor really hammered, is the part that surprised me. The
sensors are flagging way more discrepancies than the old cycle counts
caught, which sounds great until you read footnote 3 on page 22, where they
basically admit a huge chunk of the "shrink" is actually placement errors
and tag misreads. So we're not catching theft, we're catching ourselves
being sloppy. Which, fine, useful, but not what was sold.

The labor piece is what got me a little worked up. The original ROI model
assumed 11 hours per store per week of associate time freed up from manual
stock checks. The actual measured number is 3 to 4 hours, and Adina's team
is pretty candid that some of that gain is being eaten by associates having
to investigate sensor false positives. So the productivity case is roughly a
third of what we projected. When you plug the real numbers back into the
payback model the breakeven slides from 18 months to something like 38, and
that's before you factor in the maintenance contract escalator that kicks in
year two.

Now, the report isn't all doom. There's a genuinely interesting section on
customer experience metrics, basket size in pilot stores is up about 1.8
percent year over year versus 0.4 in the control group, and the working
theory is that better availability on the top 200 SKUs is doing more for the
customer than the aggregate availability number suggests. So the technology
might be helping in a way the original KPIs weren't really set up to
measure. I find that genuinely encouraging and I wish more of the analysis
had leaned into it instead of grading the project against the original
(frankly oversold) targets.

What's bugging me, and this is the emotional part I guess, is that I sat in
three of those vendor demos last year and I remember the pushback I raised
about the false positive rate in their case studies. I was told it was a
"known limitation that's been substantially addressed in the current
firmware." Reading this report it is clearly, demonstrably, not addressed.
And we spent real money on this. Not just the hardware, the integration
hours from Edith's team alone were enormous, and she had to defer the POS
refresh by a quarter to make room. So when I see the recommendation section
softly suggesting we proceed with the phase 2 expansion to 40 more stores, I
want to throw something. We have not earned phase 2. We have earned a hard
conversation about whether the tuning problems are solvable and whether the
vendor is going to actually own the firmware issues this time.

Anyway. I'm not asking you to do anything with this, I just wanted you to
have the context before Adina presents, because his deck is going to lead
with the basket size number and the shrink detection volume, and I think
both of those are genuinely interesting findings that are also being used to
paper over the fact that the core operational case underperformed. If you
read the report yourself, the sections worth your time are the methodology
notes on page 8, the SKU-velocity breakdown starting on 17, and footnote 3
on 22 which I mentioned. The executive summary is, in my opinion, slightly
too kind.

I'll probably circle back with you after the all-hands to see what you
thought, especially if any of this lands differently for the ops side than
it does for me. And if you happen to talk to Edith before then, give her a
little credit, her team's integration work is honestly the only reason any
of the positive findings exist at all.

subject: Strategy Breakdown
body:
Dave,

Finally getting around to writing this up. You asked me last week at the
offsite what the deal was with the Cornerstone deal structure and why
finance has been so heads-down on it, and I promised I'd send something more
detailed than the two-minute version I gave you over coffee. Fair warning,
this got long. I'd rather over-explain than have you walk into the ops
review next month and get blindsided by the working capital impact.

Background first. As you know, Bridgepoint has been undercutting us on the
mid-market renewal segment for about three quarters now. Their list pricing
isn't actually lower than ours when you do the apples-to-apples comparison,
but the way they structure payment terms makes the effective cost
meaningfully lower for customers who care about cash flow timing, which is
most of them. Specifically, they've been offering 24-month deferred billing
on the services component with no interest, and they're eating the carry on
their balance sheet. We've lost at least four accounts I know of where the
procurement team explicitly told us the deciding factor was timing, not
price. Theo pulled the win/loss data in February and it was pretty stark.

So the strategy Finance and Sales leadership landed on, which got board
approval in April, has three pieces that work together. I'll go through them
in order because they only really make sense as a package.

First piece. We're partnering with Acumen Capital (a specialty finance firm,
they do this kind of thing for several B2B vendors) to offer customer
financing on the services component of any deal over 250k. The customer
signs a financing agreement with Acumen, not with us. Acumen pays us in full
at deal close, less a discount factor that runs about 4 to 6 percent
depending on customer credit. The customer then pays Acumen over 24 or 36
months. From the customer's perspective this looks almost identical to what
Bridgepoint is offering, but on our side we get full recognition of the cash
up
front and we move the credit risk off our balance sheet. The discount we pay
Acumen is meaningfully less than the cost of capital we'd incur if we tried
to carry the receivables ourselves, partly because Acumen is more efficient
at collections in this space and partly because of how they fund.

Second piece, and this is the one that's clever. Because Acumen is taking
the credit risk and we're getting paid up front, we can be much more
aggressive on the structure of the deal itself. So Sales is now empowered to
offer a "ramp" pricing model where year one is discounted (sometimes as deep
as 30 percent off list) with year two and three at a small premium to list.
The blended three-year value is comparable to or slightly better than our
standard pricing, but the customer gets a much lower year-one number, which
is what hits their budget and what procurement cares about. Bridgepoint
can't
easily match this because their financing is internal, so deeper year-one
discounting actually hurts their cash position. We're essentially using
Acumen's balance sheet to fund a pricing posture our competitor structurally
can't replicate, at least not without changing how they fund the business.

Third piece. We're using the up-front cash from the Acumen deals to fund a
customer success investment program (Tobias is running it out of the
post-sale org) that's specifically designed to drive expansion in years two
and three. The thinking is that the ramp pricing creates a natural moment in
year two where the customer is paying more, and historically that's when
churn risk spikes. So we're front-loading the relationship investment to get
ahead of that. The expected expansion uplift, if we hit even half of what
the model assumes, more than pays for the discount factor we're giving up to
Acumen.

Now, the accounting on this is where it gets complicated and where my team
has been spending most of our time. A few things worth knowing.

Revenue recognition under ASC 606 is largely unaffected because we're
recognizing based on performance obligations, not cash receipt, but the
contract modification and variable consideration analysis on the ramp deals
is non-trivial. We're treating the ramp as a single contract with the
discount allocated proportionally across the performance obligations, which
means year one revenue recognition is actually higher than year one
billings. That's going to create a deferred revenue / contract asset dynamic
on the balance sheet that's going to look weird if you're not expecting it.
I've been telling people to look at billings and ARR if they want to
understand the business, and treat GAAP revenue as a lagging indicator for
the next several quarters.

The Acumen relationship gets accounted for as a sale of receivables, not a
financing, because it's true sale treatment with no recourse. That was a
long conversation with the auditors and I will spare you the details, but
the upshot is the discount factor flows through as a contra-revenue item,
not as interest expense. So our gross margin will look slightly worse on
these deals even though the economics are good. Again, something to be aware
of when you're reading the financials.

The cash flow statement is going to look great, possibly suspiciously great,
for the next two or three quarters as we ramp this up, because we're
effectively pulling forward cash that would have been collected over 24
months. I've already flagged this to IR so they can manage expectations, but
I mention it because someone in your org may notice the cash flow vs.
earnings divergence and ask questions. The short answer is it's real cash,
it's not a one-time benefit in the sense of being non-recurring (we expect
the program to keep running), but the year-over-year growth rate in
operating cash flow is going to be inflated until we lap the program launch.

There's also a tax angle that I won't get into deeply but the gist is that
the up-front recognition for tax purposes creates a timing difference we
have to manage, and we're working with KPMG on the structure. Don't worry
about it from your end, just know it's been thought about.

Risks. Two main ones. The first is that Acumen's underwriting standards may
screen out some customers we'd otherwise want to do business with, in which
case we either lose the deal or we offer them our standard terms and lose
the pricing advantage. We've negotiated a fallback where Acumen will work
with us on borderline credits at a higher discount, but there's a tail of
customers that just won't qualify. The second risk is concentration. We're
putting a meaningful portion of our customer financing through one
counterparty, and if Acumen ever has issues we'd have a real problem. We're
starting conversations with a second provider for diversification but that's
six months out at least.

Last thing. The reason I'm telling you all this in detail is that your team
is going to start seeing some operational consequences, specifically around
how deals get booked in the CRM, what shows up in the order management
system, and how commission calc works for these structures. Vera is leading
the change management on that side and I think she's planning to come talk
to your team in the next couple of weeks, but I wanted you to have the
financial context before that conversation so you're not hearing it cold.

Happy to grab thirty minutes if you want to talk through any of it. I know
this is a lot.

subject: Approval Procedures
body:
Dave,

Following up on what you asked me at the standup about how branding launches
actually get greenlit around here. It's less mysterious than it looks but
there are a few more steps than people expect, so I figured I'd lay it out
while it's fresh.

First step is the concept brief. This is a one-pager that sits with
Marketing leadership (currently Alaric, since Zara is still out on leave
through the end of the month). The brief needs the working name of the
effort, the audience, the business case, and a rough budget band. Alaric
likes seeing a competitor reference or two in there, even if it's just "we
want to look less like Vendor X." She doesn't formally sign off at this
stage, she just gives you a thumbs up to keep going. If you don't get that
thumbs up the rest of the process won't move, so don't skip it thinking
you'll fold it into a later deck.

Once you have the green light from Alaric, you build the full creative brief
and bring in Legal and Brand Standards. Legal is mostly looking for
trademark conflicts and anything that could read as a competitive claim.
Brand Standards (Elias and his team) will check that the visual direction
doesn't contradict the existing system, or, if it does, that you've got a
defensible reason. Elias is reasonable but he's been burned before, so come
prepared. Plan on two weeks for this round, sometimes three if Legal has
questions.

After that it goes to the Marketing Review Committee, which meets every
other Thursday. You submit materials by EOD Monday before the meeting or you
get bumped to the next cycle, no exceptions. The committee includes someone
from Sales (usually Andre), someone from Product, and a finance partner.
They're looking at alignment with the broader go-to-market and whether the
spend makes sense against the projected impact. Most efforts get a
conditional approval here with revisions requested, very few get approved
clean on the first pass, so don't take it personally.

For anything over $250K in total spend, or anything that touches the master
brand (logo, tagline, primary color system), you also need executive
sign-off. That goes through Alaric to the CMO and, depending on scope,
sometimes to the CEO. This is where things can stall, because exec calendars
are what they are. Build in a month minimum for this layer if you're
touching the master brand.

Last thing, and this trips people up: once you have all approvals, you still
need to coordinate the launch window with Comms and with Sales enablement.
We had that situation in Q1 where a sub-brand launch landed the same week as
a pricing announcement and it was a mess. Comms keeps a calendar, just ask
Sasha for read access and check it before you commit to a date.

Net of all that, plan on eight to twelve weeks from concept brief to public
launch for a typical sub-brand effort, longer if it's master brand. I know
that sounds like a lot but it's actually faster than most places I've
worked.

Let me know if you want me to walk through any of it in more detail, happy
to grab coffee.

subject: Team Restructuring
body:
Dave,

Okay, so I've been sitting on this for a couple of days trying to figure out
how to write it without sounding either too rah-rah or too defeated, and I'm
just going to send it because if I keep editing I'll never hit send.
Alma announced the restructure to the directors on Tuesday and the wider
marketing org gets the official memo on Monday morning, but since you and I
have been running point on the campaign ops stuff together for the last year
and a half I wanted you to hear it from me first. None of this is
confidential exactly, but please don't forward.

The short version: marketing is being split into three pods instead of the
current functional teams. Brand, demand gen, and content are being broken up
and redistributed. Each pod will be aligned to a customer segment
(enterprise, mid-market, and what they're calling "growth," which I think is
just SMB with a friendlier label). Inside each pod you'll have a pod lead,
two campaign managers, a content person, a designer or shared designer, and
an analyst. The idea, according to Alma, is that we stop optimizing for
channel and start optimizing for the customer journey end to end. On paper I
get it. In practice I have a lot of feelings, most of which I will spare
you, but a few of which are coming whether you want them or not.

I'm being moved to the enterprise pod as a campaign manager. Which, fine.
It's not a demotion on paper, my title stays, comp stays, but I built the
demand gen function basically from scratch over the last three years and now
demand gen as a thing doesn't exist anymore. The webinar program, the
nurture streams, all of it gets absorbed into pod-level execution. Nobody
owns it horizontally. I asked Alma who's making sure we don't end up
with three pods running three different versions of the same nurture and she
said "the pod leads will coordinate," which, sure, in the same way that my
houseplants will coordinate to water themselves.

You are staying in your current reporting line for now but your dotted line
shifts. You'll be supporting all three pods on the ops and martech side,
which I think is actually the right call because splitting ops across pods
would have been a disaster, but it does mean you're going to get pulled in
three directions and the pod leads are going to be territorial about your
time. We should probably talk about how you triage that before the new
structure goes live on the first. I have some ideas, mostly around a shared
intake form and a standing 30 minute weekly with each pod lead, but I want
to hear what you're thinking too because you're the one who'll actually have
to live it.

Pod leads, in case you're wondering: Zora gets enterprise (so he's my new
manager, which I'm trying to be open-minded about). Adelina gets mid-market.
The growth pod lead is being hired externally, which is a whole other thing
I have opinions about because we have at least two internal people who could
do that job and it is genuinely frustrating to watch them get passed over
again. I'm not going to name names in writing but you can probably guess.

A few practical things you should know before Monday. The campaign calendar
is being rebuilt from scratch, pod by pod, starting the second week of the
fiscal year. Anything currently in flight that crosses segments (the partner
webinar series, the Q1 product launch comms, the customer story refresh)
needs an owner assigned before kickoff or it's going to fall through the
cracks. I've started a list and I'll share it with you next week, but if
there's anything on your side you know is at risk, flag it now while we
still have leverage to assign it cleanly. Once we're in the new structure
it'll be much harder to hand things off without a turf negotiation.

Budget is being reallocated by segment rather than by function, which I
think is the part that's going to cause the most pain in the first quarter.
Demand gen historically had the biggest line item because paid media lives
there. Now that paid media gets split three ways, every pod is going to feel
underfunded relative to what they want to do, and there's going to be a lot
of "well, brand should be paying for this" type arguments. Alma says the
pod leads will work it out. See above re: houseplants.

The one genuinely good piece of news is that the analyst headcount goes up.
We're getting three pod-level analysts instead of the two shared ones we
have now, which means we might actually get attribution work done in this
lifetime. Small win, but I'll take it.

I want to say something honest here which is that I'm sad. I know that
sounds dramatic for a reorg announcement and I'm not going to make it weird,
but I really liked the team we had. The demand gen group was good. We were
doing real work. And now it's getting dissolved in the name of a structure
that some consultant probably drew on a whiteboard six months ago, and I'm
supposed to be enthusiastic about it on Monday in front of the whole org.
I'll be enthusiastic. I know how to do the thing. But I wanted to tell one
person the truth before I have to start performing for everyone else, and
you're that person, so, thanks for reading this far.

Anyway. Let's grab coffee Friday if you have time, I'm free anytime after
10. We can talk through the ops question and also you can tell me to get
over myself, which I will probably need by then.

subject: Meeting Rant
body:
Dave,

Wanted to vent a bit and also give you the rundown on what's been going on
with the cross-team meeting situation, since I know it's come up in your
check-ins too and you'll probably hear about it from Esme at some point.

So here's where I am. For the last two quarters I've been the one organizing
the standing biweekly between our team, the ops folks, and the finance
partners. You know the one, Tuesday at 10. I inherited it from Kestrel when
she moved over to the strategy group, and at the time it was already a mess
of reschedules, so I made it my project to actually fix it. I sent out a
poll, I looked at calendar availability across all fourteen invitees, I
talked individually with the three people who had recurring conflicts, and I
picked the slot that genuinely worked for everyone. Tuesday 10am is not a
slot I love, by the way. I'd rather not start my week with a meeting that
big. But it was the only window where literally no one had a hard conflict.

I also do the prep work. I send the agenda the Friday before. I confirm
attendance Monday morning. If someone tells me they can't make it, I either
reschedule the whole thing or I make sure their input is captured async so
we don't waste the meeting trying to cover their piece. My team in
particular, I've drilled into them that this is a protected slot. No 1:1s on
top of it, no skipping out for "quick syncs" with other groups, no working
from a coffee shop with bad wifi that day. We show up, on time, prepared,
with materials.

And yet. In the last six sessions, ops has had at least one no-show every
single time, and twice the ops lead herself bailed with under an hour's
notice because something else "came up." Finance has been better but they
have this habit of joining ten minutes late because their 9:30 always runs
over, which, fine, except it means the first portion of our agenda gets
repeated for them when they finally show up. Last Tuesday was the worst one
yet. Three ops people declined the morning of, the finance lead joined from
her car, and then we got bumped out of the conference room at 10:45 because
somebody else had booked it and we were running behind because, again, half
the room was missing for the first fifteen minutes.

What's frustrating is that I've raised this. I talked to Esme about it back
in, I think it was August, and he said he'd remind his team about meeting
hygiene. I talked to Linus in finance and she was apologetic and said she'd
try to move her 9:30. Nothing has actually changed. I don't want to be the
person who keeps escalating something that on paper sounds petty (people are
late to a meeting, oh no), but the cumulative effect is real. My team has
started asking me, not unreasonably, why they're being held to a standard
that nobody else seems to share. And I don't have a great answer beyond
"because I said so and because it's the right thing to do."

The HR angle on this, and the reason I'm telling you specifically, is that
it's starting to bleed into the engagement stuff we've been tracking. Two of
my direct reports flagged in their last skip-levels that they feel the
team's time isn't respected by other groups. That's not a sentence I want
showing up in the next pulse survey. It's the kind of thing that sounds
minor until you realize it's a proxy for a bigger feeling about whether the
work we do matters to the rest of the org.

I'm not asking you to do anything about it, to be clear. I know meeting
culture isn't really an HR issue in the formal sense and I'm not trying to
make it one. I just wanted you to have the context in case it comes up, and
honestly I wanted to write it down somewhere other than my own head because
I've been stewing on it for about a week. I'll probably bring it up with my
own manager next 1:1 and see if she has a read on whether it's worth pushing
harder or just letting it ride until the new fiscal year when we can rethink
the cadence entirely. There's a real argument that the meeting itself is too
big and that's the actual problem, but that's a conversation for another
day.

Anyway. If you happen to hear grumbling from my team in any of your
conversations, that's the backdrop. They're not wrong to be annoyed. I'm
annoyed too, I'm just trying to model patience about it, with mixed success.

Hope your week is going better than mine. The coffee in the third floor
kitchen has been weirdly good lately, by the way, in case you haven't been
over there. Small consolation.

subject: HVAC Shipment Delay
body:
Dave,

Wanted to give you the long version on the HVAC upgrade situation since I
know you've been getting questions about it from the third floor folks.
Short version is the parts are delayed, again, and we're now looking at late
October at the earliest for the rollout to actually start. Longer version
below if you want the gory details.

So as you know, the original plan had us replacing the variable speed drives
and the control boards on the four rooftop units (RTU-1 through RTU-4) over
a weekend in mid-September. Ardent Mechanical was going to do the install,
we'd already pulled the after-hours building access permits, and Beatrix
from
facilities had the freight elevator booked. Everything was lined up. The
drives were supposed to ship from the manufacturer's distribution center on
August 22nd.

That didn't happen. The first delay was on their end, something about a
control board revision they had to push because of a firmware compatibility
issue with a component supplier. I got the email on August 19th saying we'd
slip about ten business days, which was annoying but workable, we just
bumped the install weekend to the first weekend in October. Ardent was
fine with the new date, the elevator booking moved without issue, no big
deal.

Then this past Monday I got a call from our rep at Ardent (Amir, you've
met her, she's the one who used to work at the old Whitfield branch). She
told me the manufacturer is now flagging a further delay because the revised
boards are stuck in transit somewhere between their facility in Ohio and the
regional warehouse. She didn't have a great explanation, just that the
freight was rerouted and it'll be at least another two to three weeks before
they have stock to ship to us. So we're now looking at parts arriving
mid-October at best, and Ardent's earliest install slot after that is the
weekend of the 25th-26th.

A few knock-on things worth knowing about:

The temporary fix Ardent did back in July on RTU-2 (the one over the east
conference rooms) was explicitly described as a stopgap. It's holding fine
for now but I don't love the idea of riding it through another full month. I
asked Amir if there's anything proactive we should do and she said as long
as we keep an eye on the discharge temps and don't see any unusual cycling,
we should be okay. I've asked Beatrix to log readings twice a week instead
of
weekly until the install is done. If anything looks weird he'll loop us both
in.

Second, the budget. The PO is already cut and the parts cost is locked, so
the delay doesn't change what we're paying for hardware. However, Ardent's
labor quote was tied to the September weekend and they've now bumped their
hourly rate effective October 1st. Amir offered to honor the original quote
if we can commit to the October 25-26 weekend in writing this week. I'm
going to send her confirmation tomorrow unless you flag a reason not to. The
differential isn't huge, maybe 1,800 dollars give or take, but no reason to
eat it if we don't have to.

Third, and this is the one that might cause some noise, the building's
annual fire system inspection was scheduled for that same October 25-26
weekend. I talked to Greta in compliance and she's already moved it to the
following weekend, so that's handled, but if anyone from the safety
committee asks why the inspection date moved, that's why. I don't think
it'll come up but figured you should know in case it does.

I also want to mention that I haven't told the third-floor team about this
latest slip yet. The last update they got was that we were targeting the
first weekend in October, and I'd rather give them one clean update with the
new date locked in rather than two updates a week apart. I'm planning to
send something out Friday once Amir confirms the install slot in writing.
If you'd rather I loop you in on that note before it goes out, just say so,
otherwise I'll cc you when it goes.

One small silver lining, the delay actually gives us time to get the access
panels on RTU-3 properly cleaned out before the install, which Ardent had
asked about and we hadn't gotten to. Beatrix's going to take care of that
the
week of the 14th.

That's the whole picture as of this morning. Nothing here needs a decision
from you, I just wanted to make sure you weren't surprised if someone
mentions the new timeline before my Friday update goes out.
